content.comment_body: Hello, I have a [product_name] controller and would like to use the high-speed input to measure the speed of a flywheel via its teeth. I found this sensor: [url] Actually, I'm more interested in getting the acceleration of the flywheel. Has anyone tried something similar? Also, which input on the controller should I use to connect this inductive sensor?

Is there anyone who can assist? If measuring acceleration isn't feasible with the [product_name] software, is it possible to at least obtain speed using this type of sensor? I know that input 3 is a high-speed 5kHz input.

Hello, I've been considering another approach for my issue and would like feedback. I have a DC electric motor, and its speed is proportional to its voltage. If I attach this motor to the flywheel and feed its voltage into an analog input of my controller, could I determine the flywheel's speed this way? I also use [product_name] monitoring software, which should let me export data to Excel for speed analysis.

Hello, Continuing with my topic, I think I may have found a solution for measuring the flywheel's speed. I'm planning to use an inductive sensor for the teeth: [url] I'll then connect the output of this sensor to a frequency/voltage converter: [url] This way, I should get a voltage that changes with the flywheel's speed. My questions are: Does this setup make sense? Which input should I use for the converter's output?

How many pulses per minute are you getting? Is your sensor fast enough in terms of switching frequency? Some [product_name] controllers offer high-speed inputs; please consult the manual for details. Frequency measurement is possible with a [product_name] - see [url] (only available in German). Personally, I am not a fan of the electric motor approach. Also, make sure your sensor is fast enough. Best regards,

This program looks promising, but I'd like to generate a curve with [product_name] monitoring software. I see input I3 is a high-speed input—do I need to configure anything in the [product_name] software? The sensor and frequency-current converter I found can handle up to 2000Hz, so I should be able to detect up to 2000 teeth per second (2 teeth per millisecond). Is that correct? Edit: I realized that to achieve what I want, I'll need an analog input.

It seems like you're using the wrong tool for the task. If you need to monitor motor speed and display speed and acceleration graphs, the [product_name] controller may not be ideal. It's like trying to measure an axis diameter with a basic tape measure. Instead, consider using freeware DAQ software with a high-frequency input card—such as USB or parallel port—and an encoder for the motor. This could be more affordable and reliable.

Maybe I'm late to the thread, but I encountered similar issues recently. Your sensor's detection range is 2mm, so ensure the distance between the sensor and flywheel teeth is 1.5mm or less. The sensor you mentioned has a max switching frequency of 2000Hz (2kHz). For high-speed motors, you could apply tape to the top of each tooth and leave one tooth in its normal state, so the sensor counts that tooth for each rotation. This method lacks precision, or you can opt for a faster switching sensor for improved counting.
